title: The blessed one's righteousness endures into the coming age
english: He says that the righteousness of the one being blessed is not quenched, nor does it stop at the present, but it extends further into the age to come. In that age his horn will be exalted in glory (Psalm 111 (112):9)—that is, the kingdom of which he will be deemed worthy when he obtains the saving promises. For Scripture customarily calls the kingdom a horn.

But it is also just that those who worship lifeless things as something better and consider them divine should become like them. And this would not rightly appear to them as a curse, but as something worthy of prayer: to become gods, just as they suppose, and to possess what they admire.
For man is empty and a falsehood in his being and non-being, because even when he seems to be, he is not, but he moves about in an image of life rather than in truth.

There is need of release from the bonds of Hades, so that the God of the living and not of the dead may be our God, and we may be his ministers in the heavenly church, to which we return as we flee the bonds of death.

He takes courage as one who has been heard, and he hopes as one who will obtain help. He is strengthened by hope so as not to fear the plots of men, nor to marvel at their powers, but to foresee their fall. These things long ago concerned Israel when the other nations pressed upon it—the word is spoken hyperbolically—and after these things they concerned the church from the nations, warred upon by the uprisings of the unfaithful. For those who had believed in each nation endured the disturbances and dangers from those who did not believe, but nevertheless both these and those, having taken courage in God, conquered their adversaries.

Those who make war on those who serve God are lifted up by human power and human authorities, but those who have chosen the worship of God are encouraged by God's help and find it stronger than every strength. And most conspicuously, those of Christ defend themselves against both visible and invisible enemies through the name of the Lord alone.

He clearly hymns the manifestation of the Lord, through which salvation is restored to all, calling him God according to the Father's name and Lord according to the Son's name, because the Lord is God and God is Lord. And having appeared as Lord, he ruled over us for life, according to the words, that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living (Romans 14:9), and over his adversaries for punishment, according to the abolition of every authority and power (1 Corinthians 15:24).

He commands the establishment of a feast through a multitude of sacrifices placed on the altar, up to its horns and its other projections. But as the word advances to our sacrifices, it reveals those who, according to the type of Christ, present themselves as a living sacrifice, a sacrifice truly pleasing to God. Their multitude fills the altar up to the highest height that is joined to the heavenly angels, through the same power that both holds up the heavenly things on high and lifts up the things on earth in the manner of an altar, receiving those who approach God.

These were those who did not walk in the counsel of the ungodly, nor stand in the way of sinners, but chose the law and the journey in it. He does not say that blameless means entirely free from falling into blemishes and sins. For that was reserved for Christ and for those who share in Christ through him. But for those others, blamelessness was judged in what was within their power, by pardon from God and not by exactness concerning the commandments. For God does not demand what is not possible, but he legislates to expose what is lacking, and he concedes what is weak, since he knows it, and provides salvation through the participation in Christ, the powerful God, which was then still to come. So blamelessness befits us who live according to Christ.

Since there were very many oppositions to virtue, like stumbling-blocks on a road, he asks for their removal. For in this way a road is prepared when the hindrances are taken away, according to the words, Cast the stumbling-blocks out of the way of my people (Isaiah 57:14). For example, for the divine David a stumbling-block was the woman and the untimely encounter with the sight; for another it was food seen for pleasure, as for Esau; for another it was glory, as for Saul; for another it was a possession, as for Ahab. Against all these things there is need of God, who prepares the way, so that he may cast these things off and preserve the love of what is good, drawing off the more violent impulses of the will and, as it were, drying them up because of the inclination of nature.
But for us who look to the divine Spirit, there will be no shame, when we see ourselves joined to him everywhere and in no way shifted toward the flesh, nor brought down by a fall from on high.

title: Prayer for understanding and the path of life
english: He asks for understanding, he says, and promises that it will not be without fruit. For I will not only learn, he says, but I will also keep your statutes (Psalm 118:7-8, 119:7-8).

Aquila says, “Do not let me go astray in ignorance.” Using his desire for the law, he fears the lack of understanding that turns many people’s zeal to the opposite. Even in what they think they are doing rightly, they have stumbled, as Solomon says: “There is a way that seems right to people, but its end goes down to the bottom of Hades” (Proverbs 14:12).
For understanding does not come immediately from memory but from divine illumination. The statutes are the things that can make righteous (Psalm 118:12, 119:12).

Pride is the mother of lawlessness. Because of it they refuse to obey God’s commands, like the disobedient people who say, “We shall not be mastered, and we will not come to you any longer.” He says this to show his own eagerness before God for obedience to the commandments. Because God understands them to be guilty, he will rebuke those who are disobedient and unsubmissive through pride (Psalm 118:21, 119:21).

He prays to escape true dishonor in the sight of God, which the Lord shows to be most fearful, saying that those who put him to shame will be put to shame. Showing the opposite of this, this man of the law says here that though he is mocked by great and proud people, he does not turn away from the study of the sacred oracles and from correction by them. And a little later he says, “I spoke of your testimonies before kings and was not ashamed” (Psalm 118:22-23, 119:22-23). Such is Paul when he says, “For I am not ashamed of the gospel” (Romans 1:16).

What he himself says is a sacrifice to God—a broken and humbled heart—he now says he has fulfilled by bringing his soul down as if to the ground and humbling himself willingly. About the unwilling humiliation he says, “Our soul was humbled to the dust; our belly clung to the earth” (Psalm 43:26 (44:25)). So having brought himself forward as humbled as is fitting, he seeks from God as recompense a lawful way of life and life according to God’s word. And this very thing is also a mark of humility: not to place the good life in one’s own power but to seek it from God (Psalm 118:25, 119:25).

It is a great thing to do everything as in the sight of God, and to say these things and recount them, and to ask for revelation about them that corrects or confirms. And he will also gain benefit for others by speaking from more divine understanding and proclaiming the wonderful kindness of God that is stored up for those who act in holiness. For the one who teaches about righteousness also teaches about its end, which is stored up for it—something wonderful and unexpected, because God rewards greatly and beyond what is deserved. Paul also spoke about self-control and righteousness and the coming judgment, so that the governor became afraid (Acts 24:25). Instead of “I will meditate,” Aquila says “I will converse,” and Symmachus says “I will explain” (Psalm 118:26-27, 119:26-27).

Since the human heart lies intently upon evil from youth, God is needed to move it toward righteous commands—that is, to lead our faculty of choice by dispensations and deeds, and by the illumination of the divine Spirit (Psalm 118:36, 119:36).

Vanity is the madness about sights, the contemplation of things that do not even exist, and also the disordered imagination in the mind. Paul clarifies this when he says, “In the vanity of their mind, being darkened in understanding, alienated from the life of God” (Ephesians 4:17-18). See how it is called vanity of mind when someone has a mind and does not use it for the contemplation of realities, but hands it over to Satan who binds it. So praying for this he says, “Turn away my eyes from seeing vanities” (Psalm 118:37, 119:37). For this is the grace of God. In this way, having turned away from such contemplation, he will be able to live in the way of God, walking in it and being made alive by it. For the way is at the same time life. Therefore the Savior says, “I am the way and the life” (John 14:6).

And since the Son is the righteousness of the Father, the one who wishes to live in the Son says this: “For the righteousness of God is revealed in him from faith to faith” (Romans 1:17) (Psalm 118:40, 119:40).

He says that the only thing sufficient to comfort us in afflictions is to have the promise of true life. Bring this to completion for us. For if we have hoped in Christ only in this life, we are more pitiable than all people, because we are afflicted now and have no hope of the life to come (Psalm 118:50, 119:50; 1 Corinthians 15:19).

title: True life is bodily resurrection, not the soul's own life
english: The life to come is a living again, since we learn that the soul is not its own life, nor life in truth, if indeed the soul is not the human being. For if the soul possessed the truth of living in its life by itself, the dead thing would not have needed to live again. Therefore the Lord also said that the dead live for God, as not yet having life except insofar as it is in the power of God who gave them life. And he says that they have perished if they do not attain the resurrection, saying that he will raise up his own, so that the one from him may not be lost. And Paul likewise says, “If there is no resurrection of the dead, then those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished” (1 Corinthians 15:18). For God did not give the soul a bodiless life from the beginning, but immediately the life in the body, breathing the breath of life into the body (Genesis 2:7).
To the sinner, godliness is a ridiculous character; but to the godly person, lawlessness is horrifying, because he foresees the terror of punishment.

“To me,” he says, “the only comfort is to look at your judgments, and my gladness is your commandments taken up in song and leading to joy through melody.” And I considered this the only good, as in a foreign and alien dwelling that can have no true good, because for the stranger the things at home are longed for, and before the return to them everything is painful.

God does not fashion a human being in the manner of a modeler, even though he is said to fashion, but such as a modeler would produce, he completes by the power that works such a shaping. And the present fashionings must be referred back to that first fashioning, as in “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you” (Jeremiah 1:5). So also Job says, “You fashioned me as clay” (Job 10:9), indicating the clay-fashioning in Adam upon himself. The request in the making is a thanksgiving, very fittingly the request for the intellectual power that makes the commandments understood. About this Paul also says, “Think about what I say; for the Lord will give you understanding in everything” (2 Timothy 2:7). The request is fitting as addressed to the Creator, as if to say: Care for your own workmanship, and perfect the living being that is intellectual by understanding. And what you prepared for your own kinship, make your own through your knowledge of your wishes. Since from the beginning the human being needed a command, by which his mind was set without need of many commands, and indeed having fallen away from that one, he needs more commands to fill the greater lack.

For without training in many evils and the help of God that comes beyond hope, a person cannot be firmly fixed in virtue. For those without contest are easily shaken when a struggle comes. Therefore, having recognized in himself the firmness that comes from many hardships, he hymns the confirming providence of God. Then he asks for rest from labors, saying, “Let your mercy come to comfort me, according to your word to your servant.”

Perhaps the righteous become dead rather than living under their afflictions, so as to resemble wineskins rather than human beings, losing their breath like settling frost, but choosing what is warm and active, as he says elsewhere, “They set me in dark places like the dead of the age” (Psalm 142 (143):3). But even in such things, he says, I did not stand away from the God-taught righteousness, just as Joseph guarded his righteous self-control.
He calls promises commandments. Trusting, he says, in your promises and their truth, I seek help from you, my God.

He asks not to be handed over to the hands of those plotting against him unto death, asking for life—not yet the life eternal but the present one. He does not ask for this as an end, but as something that will contribute to a good end, because, he says, having survived, I will keep the commandments of God, through which it is possible to obtain the life eternal.

“I will follow your laws,” he says. “For I will have life in them, just as you have said to me: ‘The person who does them will live in them’ (Leviticus 18:5).” Therefore the righteous person alone lives, even if he seems to have died, and the unjust are dead even if they appear to live. For the former have the constitution of life in themselves, namely righteousness, while the latter, not having this, resemble lifeless things moved not by themselves but from outside, because their vital principle is outside, and they have not one life in themselves. Therefore the Lord, being himself the righteousness that truly is, declares himself to be the life, and says that those who do not share in him do not have life in themselves. And the death of the Savior is not only life, but also life-giving for human beings, becoming the release from death.
